Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Global Aerospace Dynamics Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, instructions for queuing up will be given at that time. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Global Aerospace Dynamics' Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are Elena Vasquez, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Reynolds, Chief Financial Officer; and Raj Patel, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Please refer to our SEC filings, including our most recent Form 10-K and 10-Q, for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those statements.

Elena Vasquez:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Global Aerospace Dynamics delivered a solid performance in Q3, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across defense, commercial aerospace, and mission services. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering long-term value to our shareholders. Today, I'll cover our key operational highlights, and then Michael will provide detailed insights into our financial results and strategic drivers.

We are particularly excited about the recent advancements in our Next Generation Air Dominance, or NGAD, program and its potential to establish revolutionary air dominance capabilities for our customers well into the next decade. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems amid global geopolitical tensions, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily with robust aftermarket tailwinds.

To start, let me touch briefly on the performance of our priority defense programs, the drivers behind our aftermarket strength, our capital deployment approach, and the key assumptions in our guidance. These areas underscore our multi-year visibility and growth trajectory. Michael, over to you for the deeper dive.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you, Elena, and good morning, everyone. I'll now turn to our priority defense programs, which continue to drive the majority of our segment growth and provide exceptional backlog visibility stretching multiple years. In Q3, these programs generated $4.2 billion in revenue, an 18% increase year-over-year, accounting for 62% of our total Defense segment revenue. Adjusted EBITDA margins improved by 220 basis points to 14.8%, thanks to a beneficial product mix leaning toward high-margin sustainment work and international sales, along with our continued progress on cost-reduction efforts even as supply chain challenges linger.

Let me break down the standout programs, beginning with our fighter platforms, which form the foundation of our portfolio. On the F-35 Lightning II program—where we act as a key subsystem integrator for mission systems and propulsion—revenues rose 22% to $1.8 billion. This was propelled by deliveries of 28 low-rate initial production Lot 17 aircraft to the Joint Program Office and our initial full-rate production Lot 1 deliveries to international partners. Our book-to-bill ratio stood at a healthy 1.4 times, with funded backlog surpassing $12 billion. Margins remained stable at 13.2%, aided by digital twin technologies that cut retrofit costs by 15% for Block 4 upgrades. From a technical standpoint, we're speeding up spiral development on sensor fusion using our Bedrock AI suite, which incorporates machine learning for real-time threat assessment. Preliminary flight tests at Edwards Air Force Base demonstrated a 40% gain in pilot situational awareness. On the funding side, U.S. DoD support is solid under the FY24 National Defense Authorization Act at $10.4 billion, but we're especially enthusiastic about Foreign Military Sales, with fresh commitments from Finland and Switzerland lifting our international delivery share to 45%.

Moving to Next Generation Air Dominance and Collaborative Combat Aircraft, our emphasis on digital engineering is paying off handsomely. We've captured a $2.1 billion tranche for NGAD demonstrator Phase 2, progressing adaptive cycle engines in partnership with GE Aerospace that aim for 30% superior fuel efficiency and supercruise capability beyond Mach 2. For CCA, we've reached critical risk-reduction milestones, including demonstrations of autonomous swarms involving 12 unmanned loyal wingmen in contested electromagnetic settings—results we presented last month at the AUSA conference. Revenues in this category totaled $650 million, up 35%, backed by a combined $28 billion backlog for NGAD and CCA. This puts us in a strong position relative to competitors like Boeing in the digital-first competitions, particularly as tensions in the Indo-Pacific spur AUKUS Pillar II funding. We've already secured $400 million in concept studies from Australia and the UK.

Our missile and precision munitions lineup delivered outstanding results, with $1.1 billion in revenue—a 25% jump—fueled by replenishment demand following Ukraine-related depletions. Our hypersonic boost-glide vehicle, featuring proprietary scramjet technology similar to the ARRW, completed a successful Mach 8 end-to-end flight test on the Pacific Test Range, securing a $900 million production contract. Javelin and TOW sustainment revenues increased 19% to $450 million, with margins at 16.5% due to automated lines at our Camden, Arkansas plant that increased output by 28%. Patriot GEM-T interceptors experienced 42% volume growth, ramping to 150 units per quarter amid Middle East conflicts—Israel represented 30% of Q3 shipments. Book-to-bill was 1.6 times here, with $15 billion in backlog through FY27, well-protected from U.S. supplemental funding uncertainties.

In naval and rotary-wing areas, Virginia-class Block V submarine module production gained momentum, contributing $550 million in revenues at 12.1% margins. We've countered 22% industry-wide steel inflation through long-term agreements with U.S. Steel, while incorporating prototypes for Virginia Payload Tube directed energy weapons to address counter-drone needs. Tailwinds from Europe are robust: NATO allies, motivated by the $61 billion Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative, have doubled orders for successors to our HELLFIRE missiles, lifting EMEA revenues by 32%.

Space and C4ISR contributed $450 million, up 14%, supported by GPS IIIF satellite sustainment and hypersonic tracking sensors for the Space Development Agency's Tranche 2. We're leading in proliferated low-Earth orbit architectures, with over 50 vehicle demonstrations that won us $1.2 billion in new task orders. Margins rose to 15.4% through model-based systems engineering, which shortened integration times by 25%.

In total, our priority programs hold an $85 billion backlog—up 12% year-over-year—with a 1.3 times book-to-bill ratio and 65% funded. Geopolitics favors us, with U.S. Future Years Defense Program growth to $849 billion and over $100 billion in allied commitments tied to NATO's 2% GDP goals. Supply chain toughness is central: we've secured 92% of critical components through U.S. reshoring, improving titanium yields to 98% from 85% in 2022. We're directing 8% of Defense R&D—$1.1 billion this year—to sixth-generation autonomy and quantum-secure communications, aligning with Teal Group's $2 trillion global A&D market projection through 2030.

We face hurdles like labor constraints in Florida and Alabama limiting capacity to 95%, and $120 million in unfavorable variances from fixed-price incentives on programs like F-15EX, but our path to 16% segment margins by FY25 is intact.

Now, shifting to the drivers of our aftermarket performance, which remains the standout element of our portfolio. In Q3, aftermarket revenues reached $1.2 billion, up 14% year-over-year and 22% organically, making up 42% of our overall revenue. Adjusted EBITDA margins climbed to 38.2%, a 210 basis point gain, powered by fleet utilization, maintenance cycles, and forward-thinking technical efforts. This highlights the durability and predictability of our services across commercial aviation MRO, engine overhauls, and defense sustainment for assets like the F-35 Lightning II and our GAD-400 regional jet fleet.

Fleet utilization is the main demand driver. Global commercial fleets are averaging 11.8 flight hours per day per aircraft, up from 9.2 hours last year and nearing pre-COVID highs of 12.1 hours. For our base of over 4,500 engines—including CFM LEAP-1A on A320neo families and GAD-X12 turbofans on narrowbodies—this means a 16% year-over-year rise in cycles. High-utilization low-cost carriers such as Ryanair and IndiGo are pushing fleets harder to capture surging travel demand, hastening wear on critical components like high-pressure turbine blades and compressor stages.

In defense, sortie rates for fifth-gen fighters have jumped 18% with elevated readiness, F-35A/B fleets at 1.2 sorties per day per aircraft. Our F-35 Joint Program Office sustainment contracts saw 12% more flying hours, spurring ALIS/ODIN-linked repairs and performance-based logistics spares. Middle East operators of our C-130J Super Hercules upgrades are up 25% in utilization due to tensions, boosting regional billings 28% year-over-year.

Maintenance cycles set the rhythm for shop visits. Commercial heavy checks—C and D visits—increased 11% to 1,450 events, with turnaround down to 28 days from 35, courtesy of our 1.2 million square foot San Antonio MRO expansion. Unscheduled removals from life-limited parts rose 9% with utilization, but our predictive tools keep in-flight shutdown rates under 0.002 per 1,000 cycles, beating industry norms.

Engine shop visits for GAD-X12 hit 2.8 per 10,000 cycles, above the 2.5 average but balanced by premium overhauls. LEAP modules are achieving 22,000 cycles time-on-wing, up from 19,500, via ceramic matrix composites. Defense fixed-wing power modules for F-35 hold at 4,000 hours mean time between depot maintenance, driving $450 million in Q3 under our Performance-Based Sustainment contract.

Regionally, North America is 55% of revenues, up 15% as U.S. carriers like Delta and United minimize deferrals with load factors over 85%. Europe grew 10%, offset by Ryanair's 737 MAX groundings but aided by Lufthansa Technik A350 work. Asia-Pacific surged 25% from AirAsia, Lion Air's 13+ hour days, tourism recovery, and COMAC C919 parts. Middle East and LATAM added 20% combined, with Emirates' A380 extensions and LATAM 787 peaks.

Our technical innovations amplify this. GAD PredictAI, blending AI prognostics with digital twins, cut unscheduled events 22% on 2,800 engines, using 95% connectivity for 92% accurate HPT forecasts up to 1,500 cycles. With Lockheed Martin on F-35 ALIS, we've digitized 70% of health monitoring, enabling predictive logistics and 15% faster mean time to repair.

We're expanding long-term service agreements to 68% of commercial base from 62%, with visibility to 2030 and utilization-linked escalators. Defense PBL backlog grew 9% quarter-over-quarter to $8.2 billion, tied to DoD's contractor logistics shift. Investments of $250 million target new Rotterdam composites repair and titanium additive manufacturing for 40% margin gains by 2026.

Forward, IATA sees 4.5% fleet growth to 2040, MRO at $110 billion by 2029 per Oliver Wyman. Defense funding keeps sorties high. Supply risks on forgings eased 30% but prices up 15%; our 180-day buffer and dual-sourcing with RTX and GE mitigate. Aftermarket guides to 13-15% full-year growth, Q4 boosted by holidays and F-35 upgrades.

Next, on our capital deployment strategy, which anchors our disciplined financial approach in this capital-heavy industry. Long-cycle efforts like F-35 sustainment, NGAD contributions, and hypersonic demand—such as ARRW analogs and our Glide Phase Interceptor—demand balancing shareholder returns with our record $152 billion backlog, up 12% year-over-year.

We prioritize strong free cash flow—105% of guidance year-to-date at $2.8 billion—and allocate across dividends, repurchases, M&A, and organic investments. This has yielded 28% total shareholder return over 12 months, beating the S&P A&D Index and peers like Lockheed and RTX.

Dividends first: Our Board raised the quarterly payout 12% to $0.58 per share, payable December 15 to November 30 record holders—our 17th straight annual hike, annualizing to $2.32 with 2.4% yield. Payout at 35% of adjusted EPS leaves room versus 45% peer average, supporting mid-single-digit growth on $10-11 billion FY24 FCF.

Share repurchases enhance EPS and reflect undervaluation at 18x forward P/E versus RTX's 22x. We added $4 billion authorization, totaling $5.2 billion to 2026. Year-to-date $2.1 billion repurchased 4.2 million shares at $285 average, retiring 1.8% float and adding 3% to Q3 EPS. Paced opportunistically, we plan $1.5-2 billion Q4 at sub-$300, targeting over 15% ROIC.

For M&A, tuck-ins expand in unmanned, directed energy, space amid USSF $30 billion FY25 and NATO $1 trillion post-Ukraine. We closed $1.4 billion SkyForge Technologies for loitering munitions like Switchblade 600, adding $450 million backlog at 20% margins. Synergies hit $80 million run-rate, merging AI into MQ-Next drones. APAC revenues up 22% to $2.1 billion on AUKUS and Japan F-35.

Pipeline includes $600 million electronic warfare for HPM threats and European missile actuators for Ukraine flows, with HIMARS/ATACMS backlog up 35% to $4.2 billion. YTD M&A $2.2 billion, 70% FCF-funded, net debt/EBITDA 1.8x.

Organic gets 25%: $900 million in DARPA turbofans for CCA and SDA cybersecurity, eyeing $850 billion FY25 DoD and Middle East Patriot demand.

With $12 billion liquidity, no debt to 2028, 8-10% FCF CAGR, we target 12-15% FY25 EPS growth.

Finally, the key assumptions underlying our guidance. Full-year 2024: $88-92 billion revenue, 9-12% organic growth, $13.50-14.50 adjusted EPS, $8-9 billion FCF. Initial 2025: 7-10% revenue growth organic, 8-12% EPS, over $10 billion FCF. Stress-tested via Monte Carlo models from F-35 and 787 histories.

Defense (65% revenue): $850 billion FY25 DoD stable, 1.1-1.2x book-to-bill on $150 billion funded/$250 billion total backlog. F-35: 150 aircraft deliveries, TR-3 IOC mid-year, $12 billion FMS. Missiles/hypersonics: 20% growth on JASSM/Tomahawk/ARRW, $8 billion awards. NGAD/CCA: $5 billion IDIQ/CRADAs. U.S. 70%, Europe 25% on NATO 2%, APAC 15% on AUKUS/Quad; 5% sequestration offset.

Commercial (25%): 6-8% RPK growth, $22 billion revenue up 12%, 1,800 deliveries, our 450 shipsets on 737 MAX 10/A321XLR. GTF delays resolve Q2 2025. Titanium $25-30/kg, 85% onshored, 3.5% labor hedged, 11-12% margins. 15% SAF aftermarket. Widebody 250 deliveries.

Mission services (10%): $9 billion, 90%+ take-up on C-130J/P-8A. 25% CAGR unmanned/space, $3 billion NASA/DoD Artemis. $500 million AI for 200 bps margins via digital twins.

Macro: CPI 2.5-3%, 70% hedged; DXY 102-105. 95% cash conversion, $4 billion repurchases, 3% capex. Downside: 10% stretch -$0.75 EPS, 5% disruption -2% revenue. Upside supplementals +$2-3 billion.

Validated by Deloitte audits, sets mid-teens ROIC path.

Thank you. Overall, Q3 revenue hit $22.8 billion, up 12% year-over-year. Adjusted EPS was $3.42. Balance sheet robust with $6.1 billion in cash equivalents. Full-year guidance unchanged. We're managing costs tightly while investing in growth, returning capital via dividends and buybacks.

Highlights: gross margin 24.1%, operating income $3.1 billion, free cash flow $2.2 billion.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from John Smith with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

John Smith:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the supply chain headwinds mentioned in the defense programs and how they factor into guidance?

Elena Vasquez:
Certainly, John. As Michael detailed, we've derisked 92% of critical tiers through reshoring, with titanium yields at 98%. Challenges like labor shortages cap us at 95% capacity, and fixed-price variances added $120 million, but our long-term supplier locks—like with U.S. Steel—and dual-sourcing mitigate this. These are baked into guidance conservatively, with buffers for FY25 stability.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Chen with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen:
Hi, thanks. I'm curious about the aftermarket outlook—any risks from regional variations like Europe groundings?

Michael Reynolds:
Lisa, great question. Regional dynamics are solid: Asia-Pacific's 25% surge offsets Europe's 10% tempered by Ryanair issues. Our 180-day inventory and LTSAs covering 68% of base provide visibility. IATA tailwinds and defense sortie rates support 13-15% full-year growth, with Q4 acceleration. Risks like forgings are down 30% YoY.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mark Rodriguez with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Mark Rodriguez:
Regarding the capital deployment—any updates on the M&A pipeline post-SkyForge?

Elena Vasquez:
Mark, we're advancing bolt-ons like $600 million in electronic warfare jammers and European actuators for Ukraine replenishment. With $5.2 billion repurchase capacity and fresh dividend hike, 55% of FCF returns to shareholders. M&A targets ROIC over 12%, funded mostly from our $12 billion liquidity, positioning for EPS growth.

Elena Vasquez:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation across our defense and aerospace portfolio.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our Q3 2024 earnings call. Slides and replay details are on our IR site.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
